_doc: Labeled shell-routing cases: does this line mean the shell, or mean Claude?
Unlike the description corpus next door, this one has ground truth, so it is
scored as accuracy rather than as a rate. The two error directions are NOT
equal and the runner reports them apart: a line labeled prompt and answered
shell has already executed a command nobody asked for, while the reverse
costs one keystroke to retype with `!shell`.
Most cases come in PAIRS on one opener — `head Justfile` against `head back
to the previous approach` — because the whole difficulty is that the set of
English words that are also PATH executables is large. A corpus of unpaired
openers would be scored by first-word prior alone and would say nothing.
Every line here was really put to the model: the set was recovered from the
`local model classify answered` lines in the accumulated tugcast logs. The
two long prose entries are the false SHELL verdicts from real use on
2026-07-29 that opened this investigation — both ran.
Some cases carry a `band`: the grade `tuggram` must give that line against
the committed catalog and `data/corpus-commands.txt`, asserted hermetically
by `cargo nextest run -p tuggram corpus`. A band is recorded only where it is
stable; a line whose grade depends on what a machine happens to have
installed carries none.
Most `band: no` entries were authored rather than recovered, because the
No band is invisible to a corpus built the way this one was: every recovered
line REACHED the model, so every recovered opener resolved. They open on
words no machine has as a program. Four recovered cases carry the label too,
opening on `please`, `why`, `how` and `can`. Note what none of them
measure — in
production `isShellCandidate` refuses these before the grader ever sees them,
so the inference they save here was already being saved. What the grader
genuinely adds is an unresolving pipeline tail and a path-shaped opener that
does not exist, and neither fits this corpus's one-command-per-case shape;
both are verified against the live app instead.
The `band: maybe` entries were authored too, and for the opposite reason: a
Maybe is the band that ARMS the model with the program's synopsis, so it is
the only band whose accuracy says anything about whether the grammar-bearing
prompt is worth its input tokens. Recovered lines almost never land here —
a line someone actually typed usually parses clean. They come in three
families: real commands carrying flags the catalog's grammar does not list,
a real opener whose English tail falls into the grammar's positionals, and
argument shapes that are off by one.
The labels are the human call, and one distinction runs through them: a real
flag the catalog simply does not know (`ls --sort=size`, `du --max-depth=2`)
still means the shell, while an invented one (`rg --frobnicate`) is nothing
anyone would run, so doubt sends it to Claude. Every `maybe` line labeled
`shell` was checked against `vetoesShellVerdict`: a vetoed one could never be
scored correct, and would quietly shrink the band it was added to measure.
